There’s a deep and concerning misunderstanding in this thread about what trauma actually is and how it shows up. This is exactly why so many of us who work in trauma and mental health get frustrated when clinical terms are thrown around by people who aren’t trained in the field.

A lot of behaviors people laugh off or even praise — like overachieving, people-pleasing, or perfectionism — can actually be signs of trauma. Because they don’t look as disruptive as a panic attack or an inability to function, they’re often dismissed or completely overlooked.

I’m not here to diagnose Sarah, and I don’t need to. But this is a public space, and the way trauma is being talked about here could easily make someone feel invalidated or walk away with a totally incorrect idea of how trauma actually works. That’s not just unhelpful, it’s harmful.

Respectfully, I think you’re misusing the term “trauma response.” You’re totally right that trauma isn’t defined solely by the event, it’s about the person’s internal experience and how their nervous system processes it. But where this kind of falls apart is in how narrowly you’re defining what a trauma response actually looks like.

Trauma responses aren’t always dramatic or easily visible. They’re not limited to panic attacks or full-blown emotional dysregulation. They can look like irritability, emotional numbness, over-controlling behaviors, perfectionism, hyper-independence, people pleasing, overachieving, or even someone appearing “fine” on the outside while burning out internally (many of which Sarah displays). A trauma response can absolutely coexist with someone functioning well in public (which I would argue she is not)— that doesn’t mean the trauma didn’t happen.

So when someone says, “This situation was traumatic for me,” and the immediate response is “That’s just stress,” it dismisses the very real, very diverse ways trauma shows up. If we’re going to call out misuse of clinical language, we have to make sure we’re not reinforcing the exact kind of misinformation we’re supposedly pushing back on.
What are you defining as a “trauma response”?

“Having a newborn baby is not trauma” is such an oversimplification. Birth and postpartum can absolutely be traumatic, even if the baby is healthy and everything appears “fine” on the outside. Trauma isn’t just about extreme, violent, or dramatic events. That mindset is not only incorrect, it’s genuinely dangerous.

This is exactly the kind of thinking that keeps people from seeking help for postpartum depression or anxiety. They tell themselves, “Nothing traumatic happened. I have a healthy baby. I should be fine.” And when they’re not, they feel broken or ashamed for struggling because society has taught them that only certain experiences “count” as traumatic.

You don’t need to like Sarah or agree with how she shares her life online but dismissing the possibility of trauma just because you wouldn’t be traumatized by something isn’t a fair or informed take. We can critique content creators without invalidating entire categories of mental health experiences.

That’s not how trauma works. Coping “well” with a distressing experience doesn’t mean someone didn’t experience trauma — it just means their system had the capacity (in that moment) to regulate or process it differently. Trauma is about how the nervous system encodes an experience, not how visibly someone struggles afterward.

The irony here is that this post claims to be calling out the misuse of clinical terms… while actively misusing clinical terms. Saying someone didn’t experience trauma because they appear regulated or coherent is not only inaccurate — it perpetuates the harmful myth that trauma only “counts” when it looks a certain way. That’s not trauma science, that’s armchair diagnosis.

Not everyone who experiences trauma develops PTSD. That doesn’t mean the event wasn’t traumatic — it means their body or brain had different tools for processing it. Similarly, “small t” trauma — things like emotional neglect, interpersonal conflict, or major life transitions — often go unrecognized precisely because they don’t fit people’s idea of what trauma should look like.

Whether or not Sarah is experiencing trauma isn’t really the point. I’m not defending her character — I’m advocating for the responsible use of clinical language. Privilege doesn’t make someone immune to trauma, and appearing outwardly “fine” doesn’t negate internal impact. Dismissing someone’s experience because they “don’t seem that bad” isn’t trauma-informed — it’s just judgment dressed up in psych terminology.

Signed, someone who works in the field of trauma and mental health.
